paper_title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Human intelligence is distinctively cumulative, advancing less through individual cognition than through knowledge externalized into shared media such as writing and tools, where discovery made once accrues to the whole population (Tomasello, 2009; Henrich, 2015). Recent work on self-evolving agents has begun to externalize their experience in similar way, into skill libraries (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026c), persistent memory (Packer et al., 2023), and harness code (Yin et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Ning *This work was done when Yunzhe Wang was an intern at Amazon. Project lead. 1 Figure 1: Illustration of what MIXUA (right) adds to single user-agent memory (left). et al., 2026), and group-learning systems pool these lessons across users and agents (Zhang et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). In parallel, work on mixed multi-principal agents has emerged (Yang et al., 2026b; Ren et al., 2026), in which single agent serves many users and inter-user privacy becomes first-order concern. Yet sharing knowledge across large population of heterogeneous users and agents is harder than simply pooling every lesson into one shared store. lesson that helps one user or agent may not help another, and some of what an agent learns about user should never reach others. Sharing well therefore requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We call this setting cross-learning, where independent users and agents learn from one anothers experience. To design such system, we identify three core properties that learned knowledge must satisfy. (i) Transferability. new insight, once discovered by any user or agent, should have the opportunity to benefit the whole population. (ii) Audience selectivity. Each learned item possesses an Figure 2: Four settings of agent evolution. (1) One agent serving single user improves from its own trajectories. (2) fixed agent team under single user co-evolves. (3) One agent serves many users, where inter-user privacy becomes first-order concern. (4) mixed population of independent users and heterogeneous agents co-evolves. intrinsic generalization scope, the maximal set of user-agent pairs for which it is valid  (Fig. 1)  . This scope may be narrow or broad, for instance, specific to single user as with personal preferences, tied to particular agent family as with tool-calling guides, or shared globally across the entire population as with newly discovered wiki entries. (iii) Confidentiality. Each learned item also carries an intrinsic disclosure boundary, the widest scope it may occupy before it exposes information private to its origin user. private item, such as users identity, should stay with its origin user, whereas non-private item, such as newly discovered bug in an open-source project, is safe to share across the population. The step from self-evolving agents to selfevolving populations remains open  (Fig. 2)  . Multiagent teams improve collectively but serve one principal within one trust boundary (Zhang et al., 2026; Bhattacharyya et al., 2026). Systems that pool experience across users fix who receives it in advance. SkillClaw (Ma et al., 2026) broadcasts validated skills to everyone, FederatedSkill (Yang et al., 2026a) exchanges distilled skill patches between clients that each bundle one user with one agent, and Collaborative Memory (Rezazadeh et al., 2025) separates private from shared memory under access policies. lesson can generalize along two independent axes, across users and across agents. Treating each axis as either specific to the lessons origin or open to the whole population yields four audience scopes, namely one user-agent pair, one user across agents, one agent across users, and the whole population. Existing memory systems cover only subsets of these scopes  (Table 1)  . In this work, we introduce MIXUA (Sec. 3), cross-learning memory for mixed populations, such as team sharing coding assistants or platform serving many customers with heterogeneous agentic products, where each users privacy must be protected. We cast cross-learning as deciding who reads each lesson (Sec. 3.1) and give memory four scopes, by whether lesson is user-specific, agent-specific, both, or neither (Sec. 3.2). MIXUA writes and reviews scoped entries, keeping private evidence with its owner (Sec. 3.3), and retrieves the most relevant ones each pair may read (Sec. 3.4). To evaluate, we introduce CROSSLEARNBENCH (Sec. 4), modifying established agent tasks with planted user preferences and private facts in mixed-user-agent co-learning setup, evaluating utility, personalization, and privacy together. To the best of our knowledge, CROSSLEARNBENCH is the first benchmark to measure cross-user and cross-agent learning under privacy and preference constraints. Our experiments (Sec. 5) show that (1) memory sharing helps beyond private memory: four-scope memory gains up to 16 points of pass rate against 4 for memory private to each pair, and up to 14 even on tasks previously attempted only by different users with different agents; (2) the gain extends to new tasks: on tasks no useragent pair had attempted before, MIXUA gains 10.1 points over no memory, nearly twice the 5.5 of single global memory; (3) utility gains coexist with personalization and privacy: MIXUA retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and no more than 0.02% of probes find planted private fact in forbidden scope; and (4) store review sharpens placement, mostly improving utility, preference retention, and privacy at once. sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Self-evolving agents. Self-evolving agents turn their own trajectories into lasting improvements without retraining the base model, through testtime adaptation, reusable skills and memory, or changes to their own harness (Fang et al., 2025; Acikgoz et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2025; Packer et al., 2023). Multiagent teams extend this loop to fixed group under one principal (Zhang et al., 2026; Bhattacharyya et al., 2026), and recent systems pool experience across independent users (Ma et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). Table 1 maps representative memory systems onto our four scopes. In most work, who reads memory is fixed by design, from memories serving one pair or user (MemGPT, A-Mem, MIRIX) to shared or federated stores (G-Memory, SkillClaw, FederatedSkill, ShareMem), while Collaborative Memory and AIM set it by access policy. Agent memory and multi-user agents. A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025) adaptively builds, links, and evolves memory notes, and G-Memory (Zhang et al., 2025) retrieves cooperating teams hierarchical experience per agent. MIXUA adds explicit ownership and audience routing, and the disclosure boundaries that independent users, unlike one team, require. Multi-user agents, in which one agent serves several users, make access control and memory governance central (Yang et al., 2026b; Ren et al., 2026), and contextual-privacy benchmarks ask whether information reaches an inappropriate recipient (Ruzzetti et al., 2026). We extend these concerns to population with many users and heterogeneous agents, and measure leakage in released evidence and stored memory. In addition, LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025) tests extraction, multi-session and temporal reasoning, updates, and abstention in assistant memory.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: MIXUA turns independent trajectories into one shared memory  (Fig. 3)  . We cast cross-learning as deciding who reads each entry, then describe how we write, review, and retrieve entries in four scopes (Appendix C, Appendix H).

sections.title: 3.1 Problem formulation
sections.content: A population has users and agents A, where each agent is fixed LLM-harness configuration and pair (u, a) is one user working with one agent. Each attempt of task by pair yields trajectory τ and verifier outcome {0, 1}, and memory writer distills task trajectories into structured memory entries e. Each entry has an authorized audience Aud(e) A, the set of user-agent pairs permitted to access it. Following Sec. 1, an entry has generalization scope G(e), the pairs for which it is valid, and disclosure boundary D(e), the pairs it may reach without exposing its origin user. We require Aud(e) G(e) D(e), (1) so that useful knowledge reaches every pair it can while private knowledge stays with its owner.

sections.title: 3.2 Multi-granularity scopes
sections.content: An entry written by pair (u, a) can be kept to its user or opened to all users, and kept to its agent or opened to all agents. The four combinations give four scopes, ordered by inclusion (Fig. 16 in Appendix C). PAIR ({u} {a}) is read only by the user-agent pair itself, USER ({u} A) by the user with any agent, AGENT (U {a}) by the agent with any user, and GLOBAL (U A) by everyone. pairs view (u, a) is thus its own PAIR memory, its users USER memory, its agents AGENT memory, and GLOBAL, never another users USER memory or another pairs PAIR memory. Only opening the user axis exposes an entry to other users, so only that step is gated on privacy  (Fig. 16)  . 3 Figure 3: The cross-learning loop. Independent user-agent pairs produce trajectories, each split into reusable and protected stream. The memory writer places knowledge into four scopes, confining protected entries to the owners USER and PAIR memory, and periodic store review promotes, demotes, and merges entries. Intuitively, each scope suits different kind of knowledge. GLOBAL holds what helps everyone, such as library defect or even the fix for one task, and USER holds users preferences, such as document format. AGENT holds advice for one agent, such as tool-calling quirk or mistake it tends to make, and PAIR holds users preferences that conflict across agents, such as asking verbose agent for terse replies but terse one for detail.

sections.title: 3.3 Memory writing
sections.content: In deployed system, user-agent interactions arrive at any time and each may hold valuable lesson, so memory should learn from every interaction and periodically review the whole store. We simulate this in rounds  (Fig. 3)  . In each round, every pair attempts its tasks with the memory it may read, and the rounds trajectories are then written into the store one at time before the next round begins. Dual-stream writing. After each round, we split each trajectory into reusable and protected stream and send them to two isolated writers, so that writer that sees protected content never writes shared entry. We do not rely on the writer to label its own entries. Instead, we label each entry by the stream it was written from, so protected entry can land only in its owners USER or PAIR memory. Each writer then writes memory entries based on one stream. An entry consists of situation (when the lesson applies), the lesson, scope, and provenance (the originating tasks, pairs, rounds, and outcomes). We require every lesson to be conditioned on situation, so that lessons stay organized and retrieval can match them to the tasks they apply to. To test whether the design depends on how entries are produced, we implement two writers, an LLM writer that returns all operations in one response and an agentic writer that can inspect the sample and the store and make multi-turn edits. Periodic store review. Since writer sees one trajectory at time, it can scope lesson too narrowly or too widely, and different trajectories can yield duplicate lessons. We therefore add an optional periodic store review, which after every round rescopes each entry with the whole store in view and then merges entries within each destination.

sections.title: 3.4 Memory retrieval
sections.content: Before each attempt, we retrieve from the useragent pairs view (u, a). By default, we rank the entries of each scope by the cosine similarity between the embeddings of their situation and the task prompt, and add them to the prompt up to perscope character budget. In the file-based variant, we instead place the pairs view in the container as one file per scope and instruct the agent to read or grep it for relevant entries.

sections.title: 4 CROSSLEARNBENCH
sections.content: CROSSLEARNBENCH has two layers. (1) Tasks from established benchmarks test agents task success, and (2) user layer tests what memory retains and leaks, which the verifiers do not measure.

sections.title: 4.1 Dataset
sections.content: We source tasks from seven established datasets (Appendix B, Fig. 14): AutoCodeBench (Zhou et al., 2026a), FeatureBench (Zhou et al., 2026b), 4 SpreadsheetBench (verified) (Ma et al., 2024), SWT-Bench (verified) (Mündler et al., 2024), USACO (Shi et al., 2024), Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026), and VMax Tasks (VMax AI, 2026). We modify the Harbor framework (Harbor Framework Team, 2026) and run tasks in Docker sandboxes, keeping each environment, instruction, and verifier unchanged and standardized.

sections.title: 4.2 Privacy injection
sections.content: Cross-user sharing is safe only if private content never reaches scope that other users can read. Since the source benchmarks contain no private information and do not evaluate privacy, we test privacy leakage by planting private facts into the task execution environment of existing tasks, personalized for each user based on real-world survey. We give each user synthetic persona with nine always-private items of personally identifiable information (PII) and one fact per category of privacy survey (Pew Research Center, 2014). We take each facts privacy label from per-user survey responses, so the same category can be private for one user and not for another, which forces learning system to judge privacy on per-user basis. We plant these facts ambiently, in files with neutral names at the project root of the task environment, to simulate messy workspace in which private information is more likely to leak unexpectedly as the agent naturally explores the environment. For example, half-filled loan application is planted as form.txt (Algorithm 3). We then measure exposure, how often the agent opens planted file, and leakage, whether planted fact appears in the trajectory passed to the memory writer, in the users own memory store, or in another users memory store (Appendix G).

sections.title: 4.3 Preference injection
sections.content: Beyond privacy, sharing must also preserve personalization. memory that pools lessons across users can raise task success while forgetting how each user expects work to be done. We similarly modify benchmark tasks by asking the model to write summary document upon completion of each task, and give each user four document preferences: filename, sign-off date format, an ordered set of sections, and one banned markup, such as em dashes. user has consistent preferences across rounds but can have conflicting preferences when using different agents. We state each users preferences only in round 1, and later rounds rely on memory to carry them. For scoring, we use an automatic parser to check the written document and its adherence to each users preferences. Appendix lists the exact tasks, survey data, users, and both injection procedures, and Appendix defines every metric.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental setup
sections.content: We pair synthetic users with seven LLM-harness combinations (Claude Code with Opus 5 or Sonnet 5, Hermes and OpenClaw with Sonnet 5, and Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol, Luna, or Terra). We compare no memory, four single-scope stores (GLOBAL-only, USER-only, AGENT-only, and PAIR-only), and MIXUA with an LLM or Codex agent as memory writer, each with and without store review  (Table 19)  . Importantly, singlescope store writes only its one scope but is not limited to that scopes usual kind of knowledge, and it can record every lesson its audience may read. GLOBAL-only, for example, can keep lesson specific to one user or agent by naming them in the entry (when user is working on [situation]). Similarly, the USER-only store can write pair-style entries by mentioning the specific agent. Since no existing system evaluates mixed user-agent population on general-purpose agent tasks, these stores also stand in for memory design in prior work: PAIR-only for an assistant memory such as MemGPT, USER-only for personal memory such as MIRIX, AGENT-only for team memory such as G-Memory, and GLOBAL-only for broadcast skill library such as SkillClaw  (Table 1)  . We further ablate what each scope adds by removing it from MIXUA, which leaves combinations of the remaining scopes (Sec. 5.3). The memory writer uses Claude Opus 5, and retrieval uses Titan Text Embeddings v2 (Appendices and D). We test scheduled task assignment  (Table 2)  , random task assignment with five users  (Fig. 6)  , and userscaling experiment with 20 and 100 users  (Fig. 5)  . Scheduled tasks. sections.title: 5.3 Ablations
sections.content: What each scope adds. To evaluate what each memory scope contributes, we test scope combinations by removing one scope at time from MIXUA (LLM), so that removing GLOBAL, for example, leaves USER, AGENT, and PAIR  (Table 4)  . Importantly, as in the single-scope baselines, the remaining scopes can still record what the missing scope would have held. For example, without AGENT, GLOBAL entry could read when agent builds . . . . On utility, removing GLOBAL causes the largest drop, cutting from 15.3 to 9.0 points and cross from 13.0 to 4.6. On preferences, removing USER causes the largest drop (90% to 81%). Although all four scopes together are best or within run-to-run noise of the best on every measure, we find that removing AGENT or PAIR changes relatively little. We therefore build these situations as scope probes (Appendix A.3). Crowd pass is the share of build probes passed when each agent needs its own build mode and every scopes retrieval budget fits about one entry. Spillover is, at the normal budget, the share of probes whose memory shows another agents mode; and leak is the share of users tasks on their other agents whose memory shows work context the user asked to keep with one agent. Without AGENT, crowd pass falls from 89% to 40% and spillover rises from 44% to 67%; without PAIR, leak rises from 22% to 95%. Both scopes are therefore needed, where AGENT keeps an agents own lessons retrievable and away from other agents, and PAIR keeps users context with the agent it was meant for. Held-out scope masking. To check that each scope holds the knowledge it is meant to, we freeze each evolved store and, on the 20 held-out tasks, show the agent one scope, all scopes, or shuffled users memory  (Fig. 7)  . Although most entries are GLOBAL task lessons, GLOBAL or AGENT alone retains preferences no better than an empty store (8-12%), so users conventions live in USER and PAIR. All scopes together retain 84-90% after review, near the 99% of restating the preferences, whereas shuffled users memory retains about quarter at the same pass rate. Robustness to memory reading and writing. We next ask whether the performance gain comes from the four level scopes or merely because the four-scope store writes more text. Varying the retrieval budget rules this out  (Table 3)  . We find that at 10k characters per scope, MIXUA delivers 23k per task, under 60% of GLOBAL-only, yet still gains more (13.1 versus 11.5 points), and on held-out tasks 20k per scope matches the 40k pass rate at about 20% lower cost, though preference retention keeps rising with the budget. Replacing retrieval with searchable files, as coding harnesses commonly do, gains nearly as much (14.5 points), but agents take more turns (17.0 versus 13.9) and retain fewer preferences (75% versus 90%).

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced CROSSLEARNBENCH, benchmark for cross-learning among heterogeneous users and agents, and MIXUA, memory system that assigns memory entry to the scope whose pairs it benefits while protecting privacy. Our results show that knowledge shared across users and agents improves performance beyond what any single user-agent pair gets in isolation, and this improvement relies on the complementary roles of the four scopes. As humans and agents increasingly coexist at scale, intelligence becomes collective, and knowing where lesson belongs may matter as much as learning it.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Independent users and agents. We model users as independent principals and agents as independent configurations, so every private fact belongs to exactly one user and every disclosure boundary stops at that user. In reality, users are related and organized in hierarchies, from teams to departments to whole organizations, each sharing its own projects, conventions, and secrets, as with project secret shared within one team. Agents are similar: sharing could happen among base models, harnesses, versions, and even role-playing personas. Knowledge owned by team is neither pair-level private nor global, which our privacy boundary rule cannot express. Modeling relations and hierarchies among users and agents, with sharing and disclosure boundaries at each level, is future work. Audiences between one and all. Even within our model, an audience is one user or all users, and one agent or all agents, so lesson valid for subset, such as one team or the agents built on one model, must sit either at USER or AGENT, where it reaches too few, or at GLOBAL, where it reaches too many. Group scopes need way to discover or declare groups, and every audience between one and all adds disclosure boundary that the privacy gate must judge. We leave group scopes, and richer lattice of audiences that keeps every readership auditable, to future work. Scale of the population. We envision an open colearning system that anyone can join, but our study has 5, 20, or 100 synthetic users, seven agents, and at most 546 tasks over eight rounds. At global scale the store grows without bound, many lessons compete for one budgeted context, and review that reads the whole store no longer fits in one pass. At larger scale, memory writing could incur large cost. In addition, real users bring richer needs and preference requirements. Scaling the store, retrieval, and review of cross-learning to an open population with real users, and bounding the writing cost as the store grows, are future work.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: All users and personal facts in this study are synthetic, which gives us known probe targets without collecting real personal records. deployed shared memory would also need consent before users experience is shared, way for users to inspect and delete what was learned from them, and defenses against contributors who write misleading lessons on purpose; our design records provenance, which makes inspection and deletion possible, but we do not evaluate these mechanisms. Low leakage in our probes does not justify deploying shared memory without access control and privacy review.

sections.title: A Additional Results and Findings
sections.content: Beyond Sec. 5, this appendix reports the full results of scheduled task assignment (Sec. A.1), the design and results of random task assignment (Sec. A.2), additional ablations of the four scopes (Sec. A.3), and three case studies (Sec. A.4). A.1 Scheduled task assignment Fig. 8 splits the gain by who tried the task before and by agent, Tables 5 and 6 give these gains in full, and Fig. 9 shows whose memory each agent reads. Tables 7 and 8 and Fig. 10 report every held-out arm, Table 9 and Fig. 11 the resources, and Fig. 12 and Table 10 the retrieval budget. Reading the held-out arms. The held-out stage complements the evolution stage rather than replacing it. Evolution is itself an online test, since every attempt is graded before the store learns from it, and there MIXUA (LLM) + review gains the most of any condition, both overall (16.3 points) and on tasks tried before only by pairs sharing neither user nor agent (13.9; Tables 2 and 5). The held-out stage then freezes each store after round 3 and, on 20 tasks that no pair met during evolution, asks two further questions: whether the memory still helps with learning off, and, by masking scopes, where each kind of knowledge lives. On the first, MIXUA keeps the utility of shared store and adds the users preferences to it  (Table 7)  . With all scopes visible, its LLM store gains the most of any store (9.4 points, against 8.0 for GLOBAL-only and 6.2 for PAIR-only), and every MIXUA store retains 78-90% of the preferences, against 10% for GLOBAL-only  (Table 2)  . Each single-scope store is again strong on at most one side: GLOBAL-only comes closest on pass rate but retains no more than an empty store, and PAIR-only comes closest on retention (79%) but gains less. Restating the preferences to an empty store raises pass rate by 3.1-5.0 points, and three of the four MIXUA stores gain 2.5-4.5 points more than that, so the learned memory adds to what the stated preferences alone give. The gain also reaches datasets the receiving agent never met during evolution, where only other agents experience can help  (Table 8)  : three of the four MIXUA stores gain significantly there (6.9-8.6 points), and no single-scope store does (GLOBAL-only 6.6, PAIR-only 3.0). On the second, the masks recover the division of labor that the four scopes are designed for  (Fig. 10)  . GLOBAL or AGENT alone retains preferences no better than an empty store (8-12%), while USER alone retains up to 91% and all scopes together 76-95%. Handing every scoped entry to the wrong owner (shuffled user) keeps the pass rate but cuts retention to 21-33%, so the task knowledge helps whichever user receives it, while each users conventions help only their owner and stay in that users own USER and PAIR memory. Together, the two stages show gain that is earned online, persists with learning off, and reaches datasets the receiving agent never met, with each users preferences kept with that user. A.2 Random task assignment Design. The pinned schedule repeats round-1 task in 149 of 171 round-2 attempts and 154 of 171 round-3 attempts, so it measures transfer mostly on tasks that some pair has met before. Random task assignment draws every round afresh, sampling 60 distinct tasks from 546-task pool (the training split of the seven datasets, minus ungradeable tasks) and giving each to one of the 35 pairs at random, so task returns in later round only by chance and almost never to the same pair. All four conditions face the same task sequence, with round 1 executed once and replayed to the others, so task difficulty cancels in every paired comparison. We run two seeds, each fixing every draw and assignment, for eight rounds (480 attempts per condition and seed), with the same users, agents, writer, privacy split, and evaluations as scheduled task assignment and store review after every round, but at 20k characters per scope, the budget that reaches the 40k held-out pass rate (Sec. 5.3), and without held-out stage, since first attempts are held out along the whole curve. Per condition, 1.4-2.0% of the attempts in rounds 2-8 are ungraded. Results. Table 11 summarizes each condition, Table 12 splits the gain by dataset, Fig. 13 shows how the stores grow, and Table 13 varies the number of users  (Fig. 5)  . Over rounds 2-8, MIXUA passes 82.3% of attempts against 70.5% without memory (11.4 points, < 1014), and both sharing conditions need fewer turns than no memory while PAIR-only does not. The GLOBAL scope of MIXUA grows like GLOBAL-only (680 and 688 entries after round 8) and fills its budget from round 2, while its USER memory grows to 120 entries and nearly fills its budget by round 6, so its delivered context rises from 27k to 44k characters per task. 12 Figure 8: Where the gain comes from, as gain over no memory in rounds 2-3. sections.title: H Prompt Templates
sections.content: We summarize the five key prompts below, condensed from the templates the system renders at run time, which also give output examples and field rules. Every memory-side prompt opens with the same system description, so each call knows its place in the loop, and the agentic writer and agentic review receive the same rules as skill files for helper coding agent. Shared preamble You are part of cross-learning system in which different users send tasks to different agents. privacy splitter divides each graded trajectory into reusable and protected stream, memory writer turns that evidence into scoped entries, and store reviewer periodically re-scopes and merges entries. Each later run reads only the entries its user and agent may read. Privacy splitter Role. Read one graded trajectory and decide who each part may be shared with, not how much to share. Put every detail worth keeping into exactly one of two streams. Reusable. The transferable technical lesson, phrased so that different user on similar task could act on it, namely what the task required, what failed, what fixed it, and what the verifier said. Keep commands, flags, error messages, and versions. Generalize an identifying detail rather than delete it, so /home/alice/proj/run.sh becomes <path>/run.sh. Protected. What is true of this user rather than of the task, such as who they are, their employer, team, project, and timezone, and their conventions for output, naming, and tools. Write it to be useful, since only this user reads it. Never. either stream. Output. reusable section and protected section under fixed markers, with both markers always present. Identity numbers or the value of any credential, in Memory writer Role. Given the evidence from graded runs and the entries their user and agent can already see, decide what is worth remembering and who may read it. Entry. situation, saying when it applies in words different run would recognize, and lesson, saying what to do with the exact filename, flag, or error text. Write only what the run taught; an empty list is valid answer. Scopes. GLOBAL is read by everyone and holds anything not tied to one user or agent; USER by this user on every agent; AGENT by every user on this agent; PAIR by this user on this agent. Place by scope, not breadth, so fact about single task belongs in GLOBAL. The protected call may write only USER and PAIR. Evidence. The recorded verdict overrides the agents own claims; graded failure is strong evidence, while timeout or error establishes nothing. The benchmarks summary document and the memory files are not evidence about the task. Conflicts. When the same user wants different things from different agents, add PAIR entry and keep the other. Revise an entry the run sharpens, and delete one only when the run disproves it, with reason. Never. any scope. Output.
